claims.text: Nearly equiatomic five-transition-metal HENA nanoparticles are intrinsically structurally unstable at elevated temperatures.
Their nanoscale instability results from surface-energy effects dominating configurational-entropy stabilization.
A high surface-to-volume ratio amplifies the driving force for phase segregation in these nanoparticles.
Nanoscale surface effects overcome the sluggish-diffusion and high-entropy stabilization mechanisms associated with bulk HEAs.
The proposed initial nanoparticles contain five metals at 20 at.% each, exemplified by CoCrFeMnNi.
The proposed initial particles have grain sizes below 10 nm and a single-phase FCC or BCC structure at room temperature.
Annealing is proposed at 500–1000 K for 1–100 hours under vacuum or inert gas.
Surface-driven atomic diffusion and evolution of chemical short-range order facilitate phase separation and grain coarsening.
High surface energy reduces the effective activation barrier for atomic diffusion in HENA nanoparticles.
Reduced diffusion barriers produce accelerated atomic diffusion relative to bulk HENAs.
Accelerated diffusion segregates elements into lower-energy phases, including BCC/FCC decomposition products.
Reduction of total surface area drives grain growth in the nanoparticles.
Annealing will rapidly destroy the initial single-phase structure and form secondary phases, intermetallics, or elementally segregated regions.
At 700 K, the particles will exhibit grain growth beyond 50 nm within hours.
The predicted structural evolution will degrade the nanoparticles' mechanical and thermal properties.
Bulk HENAs retain single-phase structures and fine grains and possess exceptional thermal stability up to 1000 K.
High configurational entropy, lattice distortion, and sluggish diffusion are responsible for bulk-HEA thermal stability.
The instability hypothesis is not expected to apply to nanoparticles larger than 50 nm because bulk-like behavior dominates.
The hypothesis may fail for compositions with strongly negative mixing enthalpies that favor ordered phases.
Experimental information on the elevated-temperature behavior of HENA nanoparticles is limited, and existing models may not capture size and element-specific effects.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify ambient pressure while also allowing vacuum annealing; vacuum is not ambient pressure unless the phrase is intended only to exclude applied mechanical pressure.
